title: What Photos Does a Small Business Website Need?
description: Plan useful small business website photos by buyer question, page role, crop, permission and alternative text instead of collecting generic images.
summary: Follow a fictional Varanasi pottery workshop as it turns a crowded camera roll into a purposeful website photo brief and shoot list.
body:
What photos does a small business website need? There is no universal number. Start with the questions a suitable visitor must answer, then assign one useful image to each job: recognise the business, understand the offer, see the process, judge fit and take the next step.

A strong photo library is not the largest folder. It is a set of original images with a known page role, enough space for the intended layout, recorded permission, a useful filename and an accessibility decision. Capture a wide and a close version of important scenes so the design can work across desktop and mobile without hiding the subject.

Asha has many photos but no usable hero image

Imagine Asha runs a fictional pottery workshop in Varanasi. The business, owner and situation are original planning examples, not a SiteSutra client story or reported result. The workshop offers small group classes and sells selected pieces from its studio.

Asha's camera roll contains finished cups, festival posts, screenshots, close views of clay and several photographs with text placed over them. The images are genuine, but the website team cannot tell which class they show, whether the people pictured agreed to website use or where a heading could sit without covering the work.

She stops asking which photos look best and gives every planned image a visitor question. The new brief follows five roles: recognise, understand, trust, choose and act.

Build the shot list around five photo roles

Asha's hypothetical website photo brief
Photo roleVisitor questionPossible subjectBrief note
RecogniseAm I looking at the right business?Studio entrance, sign or owner in the actual spaceWide view with uncluttered space for a heading
UnderstandWhat does the business offer?Class setup, finished pieces or a clearly named serviceShow the offer, not a generic decorative object
TrustHow is the work done?Hands shaping clay, tools, materials and a tidy work areaRecord what the scene proves and who may appear
ChooseIs this suitable for me?Class size, seating, access details or product scaleInclude details that affect the decision
ActWhat happens when I enquire or visit?Welcome point, consultation table or collection areaPlace near the matching call to action and instructions

These roles are a planning method, not a requirement for five photographs. One strong image can answer more than one question, while a complex service may need several views. The brief should explain the job before the camera is used.

Plan the hero image for the layout it must support

Asha wants the homepage heading to remain readable on a large screen and a phone. Her brief asks for a wide studio scene with the potter and wheel away from one edge, plus a closer vertical version for a narrow crop. She also captures the scene without text, stickers or a social media frame.

The designer can then choose a crop without removing the subject or placing important words over a face. A single tightly framed portrait would be attractive, but it would not give the same layout options.

Show the real offer without turning the page into a gallery

The service page does not need every finished piece. It needs enough visual evidence to explain the class: the work area, the material, a step in the process and a finished example. Captions name what the visitor is seeing instead of repeating “our work”.

Asha separates commissioned work, classroom scenes and products. She records whether each image is hers to publish and whether a person, customer location, artwork or identifying detail needs approval or removal. When permission is unclear, the image stays out of the public site until the business resolves it.

Send original files with context

A useful handover includes the original image file, not a screenshot or a copy downloaded from a social platform. Asha gives files short descriptive names, groups them by planned page and adds a sentence explaining the scene. The website team keeps the original outside the public build and creates suitable delivery versions.

Google's image guidance recommends relevant, clear images near matching page text, descriptive filenames and contextual alternative text. It also notes that images can add substantial page weight, so responsive image techniques help balance quality and loading. These practices improve implementation quality; they do not guarantee search visibility or clicks.

Decide alternative text from the image's purpose

Alternative text is not a hidden keyword list. The W3C decision tree asks whether an image contributes meaning, performs a function, repeats nearby information or is purely decorative. The answer depends on the specific page context.

For the class page, “Hands centring clay on a pottery wheel during a beginner workshop” can communicate useful information when that action matters. A decorative texture that adds no information should use an empty alternative text value so it does not create noise for a screen reader. A complex diagram needs its essential information available in text as well.

Open the situation closest to your photo library

Each prompt turns a common asset problem into a concrete next action.

I only have photos from Instagram or WhatsApp

Return to the phone, camera or photographer archive and look for the original files. Record the scene and intended page. If only a compressed copy exists, test whether it remains clear at the required display size and plan a replacement rather than inventing detail.

Customers or team members appear in the photos

Record who appears, where the image will be used and whether the business has clear permission for that use. Remove private screens, customer details and identifying information that the page does not need. Keep the permission record outside the public website repository.

I have no professional photographs yet

Prioritise a small honest set: the real place or setup, the owner or team where relevant, the offer, the process and the next step. Use clear light and a tidy scene. Label any temporary image in the project plan and avoid publishing a stock image as if it shows the business.

The same image must work on desktop and mobile

Capture important scenes in wide and vertical compositions, with useful space around the subject. Ask the developer how responsive sizes and crops will be delivered, then inspect both layouts before approval.

Turn the camera roll into a photo brief

Download the small business website photo brief (CSV). For each planned image, record the page, visitor question, subject, orientation, permission status, original filename, crop note, alternative text decision and readiness.

Do not place private customer details, personal consent records, confidential locations or account information in this public template. Store sensitive records through an approved private process.

Photograph the missing decision, not more of the same

Asha does not discard her camera roll. She identifies the useful images, records their purpose and makes a short reshoot list for the missing visitor questions. The website can now show the actual workshop without forcing one photograph into every shape or implying permission that was never checked.
